title: The College ROI Map
summary: Top 20 vs 21–50 vs 51–100 — how cost, salary, and payback actually compare across college tiers, and when prestige rank genuinely matters for career ROI.
text: The Big Question The Hypothesis Top 20 may justify a premium. From roughly 20–100, outcomes often overlap more than people think. What Drives ROI Net price, major, graduation rate, internships, and career placement often matter more than rank alone. The Big Trap Paying full price for prestige can destroy ROI if debt gets too large. The Big Advantage Elite schools can offer stronger networks, recruiting, and grad-school pipelines. The Real Test Compare expected debt against first-year salary and compare net price, not sticker price. · The ROI Comparison: Top 20 vs the Next 80 Tier Typical Published Annual COA Typical Net Price Range Avg Early-Career Salary ROI Pattern Bottom Line Top 20 $80k–$92k $28k–$70k $82k–$100k Highest upside; strongest recruiting and brand signal Worth paying a premium only if debt stays reasonable or aid is strong. Ranks 21–50 $55k–$88k $22k–$55k $72k–$88k Strong outcomes; more overlap with Top 20 than many assume Often the sweet spot when scholarships or flagship-public pricing are available. Ranks 51–100 $30k–$75k $18k–$45k $65k–$80k Wide dispersion; great value schools can beat pricier schools above them Usually choose best fit + lowest cost + strongest major outcomes. · Illustrative 2025 estimates based on published cost of attendance ranges, salary reports, and college ROI research. Results vary by major, residency, and aid. · Is 20–100 Basically the Same? Partly True From about 20–100, the ranking premium flattens. A strong public flagship, honors college, or scholarship-heavy option can produce similar or better ROI than a more expensive private school. Not Totally True The best schools in the 20–40 band still tend to have stronger recruiting, alumni networks, and placement in finance, consulting, tech, law, and elite graduate programs. The Real Take Beyond the very top tier, rank matters less than debt load, major, internship access, graduation rate, and personal fit. · Where Rank Matters Most — And Least Career Path How Much Prestige Matters Investment banking / elite consulting Very high Quant / top tech / selective finance High Law / medicine prep Moderate to high Engineering / computer science Moderate — school matters, but strong publics can compete well Accounting / nursing / teaching Lower — licensure, skill, and debt usually matter more Entrepreneurship / general business Moderate — network matters, but execution matters more · Pay Whatever It Takes? Not Exactly If a Top 20 school gives great aid, lean yes. If total debt will exceed expected first-year salary, be cautious. If a strong in-state public or honors option costs far less, compare ROI hard. For finance, consulting, and certain elite pipelines, a Top 20 premium is more defensible. For many majors, the cheapest high-quality option wins. · Practical College ROI Bands Best Value Zone Strong public flagship / honors / scholarship school. Goal: high outcome, low debt. Smart Prestige Zone Top 20 or Top 30 with meaningful aid. Goal: use prestige without wrecking ROI. Caution Zone Expensive private without enough aid. Goal: avoid overpaying for a small ranking bump. Red Flag Zone Heavy debt for unclear career upside. Goal: do not finance prestige at any cost. · The right college is not the highest rank you can get into — it is the best long-term return on your talent, goals, and finances. · Educational infographic only. Not financial, legal, or admissions advice.

title: Decoding George Tritch's Periods to Make Money
summary: A 19th-century market-cycle framework of panic, good, and hard-time periods — read as a historical lens on sentiment, not a timing system.
text: The Big Idea A Historical Market Map A 19th-century cycle framework attributed to George Tritch and closely associated with Samuel Benner. Three Signal Types The model classifies markets into panic years, sell years, and buy years. B = Good Times to Sell The chart says prosperity and high prices are often the time to trim risk and take gains. C = Hard Times to Buy The framework treats low-price periods as opportunity zones for accumulation. Use as a Lens, Not a Law Interesting historically, but not a standalone investing system. · The Tritch Cycle Decoded A Periods Panic Years Meaning: panics, reversals, or bear-market stress Classical rhythm: 16/18/20-year sequence Investor posture: caution, defense, liquidity Modern translation: reduce fragility; avoid overconfidence B Periods Good Times / High Prices Meaning: prosperity, optimism, elevated pricing Classical rhythm: 8/9/10-year sequence Investor posture: rebalance, trim, harvest gains Modern translation: don't confuse euphoria with safety C Periods Hard Times / Low Prices Meaning: depressed prices and opportunity Classical rhythm: shorter recurring bottoming windows, often described as 3-6, 2-5, and 4-7-year sub-cycles Investor posture: accumulate quality assets carefully Modern translation: buy when fear is highest, if fundamentals hold · Traditional descriptions of the cycle are historical interpretations and should be treated as illustrative rather than precise market forecasts. · How Investors Try to Use It Identify the phase Ask whether the market feels panicky, euphoric, or washed out. Match the posture Defend in A, harvest in B, accumulate in C. Check the fundamentals Use valuations, earnings, rates, and breadth — not the cycle alone. Size risk carefully Never bet the portfolio on one timing model. Rebalance disciplined Use the cycle as a sentiment overlay, not a prophecy. · What the Framework Gets Right vs. What It Misses What the Framework Gets Right Markets Are Cyclical: booms, busts, and sentiment swings do repeat Extremes Matter: the best opportunities often appear when emotions are extreme Selling Is Part of Investing: taking gains and rebalancing is underrated Buying Fear Takes Courage: long-term wealth often comes from disciplined buying in weak periods What It Misses / Big Caveats No Guarantees: real markets rarely obey neat calendars Dates Drift: even if cycles rhyme, exact turning points are unreliable Macro Changes: rates, policy, technology, and geopolitics can overwhelm old patterns Valuation Still Matters: cheap and expensive are more useful than mystical timing Good Risk Management Wins: diversification and discipline matter more than prediction · Practical Money Map Takeaways Accumulation mode Use C-like weakness to buy quality assets steadily. Rebalance mode Use B-like strength to trim winners and restore allocation. Defense mode In A-like stress, protect liquidity and avoid forced selling. All-season mode For most investors, systematic investing beats trying to perfectly time every turn. · The value of Tritch's map is not perfect prediction — it is the reminder that markets move in cycles, sentiment swings, and disciplined investors prepare for both. · Educational infographic only. Better opportunity exists A higher-quality or higher-return opportunity is available elsewhere. Cash or tax need Need liquidity for goals or obligations, or to manage taxes more efficiently. · The Selling Ladder Partial trim When position grows far above target allocation. Harvest tax losses When useful and compliant. · Great selling is usually staged, not emotional. · Sell Signal Decision Matrix Signal Action Why Blow-off top / euphoric spike Trim or scale out Reversals after euphoria are frequent and drawdowns can be sharp. Fair value exceeded by a wide margin Trim or reduce Lower future returns likely when price is far above fair value. Guidance cut / earnings miss Reduce or exit Signals weakening fundamentals or deteriorating outlook.
